description: Synthetic sales activity bank for LeadBrief seeding. Bodies were generated by an LLM (Claude) and reviewed manually. Golden contacts are NOT in this file.

notes.subject: Intro call
notes.body: Intro call with {first_name}. They run sales ops at {company} with a team of 12 reps. Main pain: reps spend too much time digging through old emails before calls. Currently using spreadsheets plus a basic CRM. Wants to see something before end of quarter.
{first_name} came in through the webinar signup. Downloaded the onboarding guide twice. Worth a cold follow-up.

notes.subject: Following up on your webinar question
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, thanks for joining the webinar on Thursday. You asked how we handle data from multiple inboxes, happy to walk you through it on a 20 min call. Does early next week work for you?

notes.subject: Discovery call
notes.body: Disco call w/ {first_name} ({job_title}). 3 regional teams, no shared view of account history. Leadership complains that handoffs between SDRs and AEs lose context. Budget not defined yet. Asked for a short deck to share internally.

notes.subject: Discovery session
notes.body: Met {first_name} {last_name} and two people from their revenue team. They are evaluating tools this quarter. Key requirements: SSO, Salesforce sync, and audit logs. Decision expected in about 6 weeks. {first_name} seems to be the champion but not the final signer.
LinkedIn connection accepted. {first_name} posted about struggling with rep ramp time. Good angle for outreach.

notes.subject: Quick intro
notes.body: Short call, {first_name} only had 10 minutes. Confirmed they have about 40 sellers. Interested but busy with a reorg. Asked me to call back in two weeks.

notes.subject: Re: Intro
notes.body: Thanks {first_name}. As promised, attaching the one pager. Short version: we pull notes, calls and emails into one timeline so your reps walk into every call prepared. Let me know if a demo makes sense.

notes.subject: Discovery call
notes.body: Spoke with {first_name}. They tried a competitor (Nimbalo) last year and dropped it because adoption was poor, reps never logged anything. Very sensitive to anything that adds data entry. Need to position as zero extra work for reps.

notes.subject: Inbound lead
notes.body: Inbound form from {company}. Free text said: "need better call prep for our AEs". Company size 200 to 500. Routing to me.

notes.subject: Coffee chat
notes.body: Coffee with {first_name} at the conference. Not a formal meeting. They mentioned their VP of Sales is pushing for better forecasting and better notes hygiene. Swapped cards, will follow up.

notes.subject: No answer
notes.body: Called {first_name}, no answer. Left voicemail referencing the webinar.

notes.subject: Checking in
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, I know things get busy. Just checking whether improving call prep is still a priority for your team this quarter. If timing is off, no problem, tell me when to circle back.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} confirmed the main KPI they care about is conversion from first meeting to opportunity. Currently around 18 percent, they want 25. Reps prepare calls by searching Gmail, takes 15 min per call on average according to them.
Research: {company} opened a new office last month and is hiring 8 AEs. Growth signal, good timing for outreach.

notes.subject: Discovery call
notes.body: Long chat with {first_name}. Their main issue is not tooling, it is that nobody writes notes. Asked if we can pull from call recordings. Told them yes for transcripts they already have. They use a dialer that exports transcripts.

notes.subject: Questions before our call
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, to make the most of Tuesday, could you share roughly how many reps would use this and which CRM you are on? That way I can tailor the demo instead of showing everything.
{first_name} replied: 25 reps, HubSpot. Wants to include their sales manager in the demo.

notes.subject: Intro call
notes.body: Intro with {first_name}, {job_title}. They are early, just exploring options. No budget this year, maybe next fiscal. Will keep warm.

notes.subject: Discovery workshop
notes.body: Ran a 45 min discovery workshop with {first_name} and the enablement lead. Mapped their current call prep: CRM record, then email search, then Slack search, then asking the previous owner. 4 sources, no single view. They loved seeing it on a whiteboard.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} is skeptical about AI summaries. Had a bad experience with a tool that "made things up". Asked how we cite sources. Explained every statement links back to the original note. Interested in seeing that specifically.
Mutual connection: {first_name} worked with one of our current customers before. Could ask for a reference intro later.

notes.subject: Re: Pricing question
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, pricing depends on seats and the plan. For a team your size it usually lands in the mid range of our pricing page. Happy to go into detail once we confirm the use case fits.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Talked to {first_name} about data residency. They have EU customers and need data to stay in the EU. Need to confirm with our product team before going further.

notes.subject: Follow-up needed
notes.body: Need to confirm EU hosting option for {company} before next call.

notes.subject: Discovery call
notes.body: {first_name} wants to understand integrations first. Uses Outlook, Zoom, and Pipedrive. Asked whether we support Pipedrive natively. Told them we have an API and a partner connector. Not thrilled about the connector.

notes.subject: Intro meeting
notes.body: First meeting with {first_name} {last_name}. Friendly, very data driven. Asked for case studies with numbers. Said the CFO will only approve with a clear ROI story.

notes.subject: Case studies
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, attaching two case studies from teams of similar size. The second one is closest to your setup, they cut call prep time roughly in half. Happy to connect you with their sales manager if useful.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} mentioned a security review will be required for any new vendor. Process takes 3 to 4 weeks on their side. Sent our security overview.
Sent security questionnaire template to {first_name}. Waiting on their version.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Second discovery call. {first_name} brought their RevOps analyst. Analyst asked a lot about how we store embeddings and whether customer data trains any model. Answered no training on customer data. Analyst seemed satisfied.

notes.subject: Cold call
notes.body: Cold call to {first_name}. Picked up, polite, said they just signed a 2 year deal with another vendor. Not a fit right now. Ask again in 18 months.
{company} not a fit for now, locked into another vendor. Set reminder for later.

notes.subject: Intro from our mutual contact
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, our mutual contact suggested we talk. We help sales teams prepare for calls by putting every note, email and meeting about a contact in one place. Would you be open to a short intro?

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} said the real problem is churned accounts coming back and nobody remembering why they left. Wants history across account owners. Good use case for us.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Met {first_name} on site. Saw their sales floor. Reps keep sticky notes on monitors with key client facts, honestly a perfect visual for our pitch. Took notes on their workflow.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} asked how long implementation takes. Explained 2 to 3 weeks for standard setups. They need it running before their sales kickoff in about 2 months.
{first_name} forwarded my email to their VP of Sales. Good sign.

notes.subject: Re: Forwarded
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, thanks for looping in your VP. Happy to set up a short call with both of you whenever works.

notes.subject: Discovery call
notes.body: Spoke to {first_name} for 30 min. Team of 8, very small, founder led sales. Price sensitive. Might be better fit for the starter plan.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} explained they lost two big deals last quarter because the new AE didn't know about promises made by the previous AE. That is their burning pain.

notes.subject: Champion?
notes.body: {first_name} seems motivated and has influence. Possible champion. Need to confirm who signs.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Asked {first_name} who signs off. Answer: CRO for anything above 20k, otherwise sales director. We'll likely land under 20k for a pilot.

notes.subject: Summary of our call
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, quick recap: 1) pain is losing context when accounts change owners, 2) about 15 reps involved, 3) decision by end of quarter. Next step is a demo with your sales director. Let me know if I missed anything.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} is new in the role, joined {company} 2 months ago. Still learning their stack. Wants to make an impact fast. Open to a pilot.

notes.subject: Lunch
notes.body: Lunch with {first_name}. Mostly relationship building. They mentioned budget planning happens in November.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} mentioned they're also talking to Corvexa. Asked what makes us different. Explained citations to source notes and that we run on their data only. They will compare.
Competitor in the {company} deal: Corvexa. Prepare comparison sheet.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} cares a lot about mobile. Field reps check info from their phone in the parking lot before meetings. Need to show mobile view in the demo.

notes.subject: Mobile access
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, good news, the brief works on mobile browsers. I'll include it in the demo so your field team can see what it looks like before a visit.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Talked to {first_name} about volume. Around 3,000 active contacts, each with maybe 20 activities. Asked if search stays fast at that size. Said yes, and we can share numbers.
{first_name} asked about performance at around 60k activities. Get numbers from product.

notes.subject: Discovery call
notes.body: {first_name} is the IT manager, not sales. They got asked to evaluate tools. Mostly technical questions: SSO, SCIM, API limits. Need to bring a solutions engineer next time.

notes.subject: Technical discovery
notes.body: Technical discovery with {first_name} and our SE. Covered SSO with Okta, API rate limits, and data export. No red flags. {first_name} will write a summary for their sales VP.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} said "honestly we just need reps to stop asking each other the same questions". Their Slack is full of "does anyone know the history with X". Strong pain.
Good quote from {first_name} for the business case: reps keep asking each other for account history in Slack.

notes.subject: Next steps
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, thanks again for your time. As discussed, I'll send a demo invite for next week including your sales manager. In the meantime, here is a 2 minute video of the brief view.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} wants a trial instead of a demo. Explained we do guided pilots with their data rather than open trials. They were OK with that.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Brief call. {first_name} confirmed interest but needs to finish a CRM migration first. Probably 6 to 8 weeks out.
{company} on hold until their CRM migration ends.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} said their reps are mostly bilingual and many notes are in Spanish. Asked if we handle mixed languages. Need to check.

notes.subject: Language question
notes.body: {first_name}'s team has notes in English and Spanish. Check multilingual support before demo.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Met {first_name} and their head of customer success. Interesting, CS wants the same thing for renewals. Possible expansion beyond sales later.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} mentioned a hard compliance rule: no customer data can go to third party AI APIs. Explained our option to run models in their own environment. That got their attention.

notes.subject: Re: Compliance
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, confirming what I said on the call: we can run with models hosted in your environment, so no customer data leaves your infrastructure. Our SE can walk your security team through the architecture.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} is very busy, kept the call to 15 min. Key points: 20 reps, Salesforce, wants a demo for their manager. Send times.
Sent 3 demo slots to {first_name}.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} described their current call prep as "chaos". New hires take 3 months to learn account histories. Wants to cut ramp time.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} said they already have a homegrown tool built by an intern years ago. Nobody maintains it. Open to replacing it but worried about migrating old notes.

notes.subject: Migrating old notes
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, regarding your old tool, we can import historical notes from CSV. If you can export a sample, we can show you how they'd look in the timeline during the demo.
{first_name} sent a sample export with 200 notes. Forward to SE for demo prep.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Spoke to {first_name}. They want to understand who else in their industry uses us. Shared two logos we're allowed to mention.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Discovery meeting with {first_name}. They have a strict procurement process, 3 quotes required for any software purchase. We are one of the three.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} asked if we integrate with their calendar so the brief is ready before each meeting. Said yes, that's on the roadmap. Careful not to overpromise dates.
Don't promise calendar integration date to {company}. Roadmap only.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} is a {job_title}, influential but no budget. Needs to convince their director. Asked for material to help them sell internally.

notes.subject: Material for your director
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, attaching a short business case template with the numbers we discussed. Feel free to edit it before sending to your director.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: Talked to {first_name}. They're consolidating vendors this year, so any new tool needs to replace something. Possible replacement: their call notes plugin.

notes.subject: Discovery
notes.body: {first_name} confirmed timeline: want something live before Q1 planning. That gives us about 10 weeks.
Asked {first_name} for their org chart for the sales team. They said they'd send it.

notes.subject: Product demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name} and their sales manager. Showed the timeline and the brief. Manager liked that each statement links to the source note. Question about how often data syncs, answered every few minutes. Positive overall.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo went OK but not great. {first_name} kept asking about forecasting features we don't have. Need to reset expectations, we're about call prep, not forecasting.

notes.subject: Thanks for the demo
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, thanks for your time today. Recording and slides attached. You asked about bulk import, here is the doc on CSV import with validation. Let me know what your team thought.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} said the team liked the demo but one rep asked "what if the summary is wrong". Explained citations again and that the brief says when there isn't enough context. They want to test that with their own data.

notes.subject: Demo for sales team
notes.body: Demo for 6 reps at {company}. Lots of questions about mobile. One senior rep was skeptical: "I already know my accounts". Fair, the value is bigger for new reps and handoffs.
Demo feedback from {company}: senior reps skeptical, new hires excited. Position around ramp time and handoffs.

notes.subject: Technical demo
notes.body: Technical demo with {first_name} and their IT team. Covered SSO setup, permissions by team, and data export. IT asked for a sandbox. Requested one from our SE team.

notes.subject: Sandbox access
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, your sandbox is ready. Credentials will come in a separate email. It's loaded with sample data so your team can explore without connecting real accounts yet.

notes.subject: Post demo
notes.body: {first_name} called after the demo. Their VP missed it and wants a 20 min version. Scheduling for next week.

notes.subject: Executive demo
notes.body: Short demo for the VP of Sales at {company}. VP cared about two things: adoption and whether it helps forecast accuracy. Focused on adoption. VP asked for a pilot proposal.

notes.subject: Pilot requested
notes.body: {first_name}'s VP asked for a pilot proposal. Prepare scope: 10 reps, 6 weeks, success metrics.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}. Their screen share kept freezing, cut it short. Rescheduled the second half.

notes.subject: Demo part 2
notes.body: Finished the demo with {first_name}. Showed question answering: "what objection did they raise last time". They loved it, asked to try it on real accounts.

notes.subject: Demo recording
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, here's the recording of today's session in case your colleagues want to watch it. The Q and A part starts around minute 18.

notes.subject: Demo debrief
notes.body: Debrief with {first_name}. Concerns: 1) price, 2) whether reps will actually open the brief before calls. Suggested a Slack notification with the brief link before each meeting.

notes.subject: Custom demo
notes.body: Built a custom demo with {company} sample data. {first_name} recognized some of their own accounts and got visibly more engaged. Lesson: always use their data when possible.
{first_name} asked for a comparison against Corvexa after the demo. Send the comparison sheet.

notes.subject: Comparison with Corvexa
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, as requested, here's a side by side. Main differences: every claim in our brief cites the source note, and we can run without sending data to third party AI services. Happy to discuss.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo for {first_name} and the CS lead. CS lead asked if we can generate briefs for renewal calls too. Yes, same mechanism. Expansion opportunity noted.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} said the demo was "the first AI tool that didn't try to sound smarter than it is". Liked that it says when it doesn't know.
Great quote from {first_name}: liked that the tool admits when it lacks context. Use in positioning.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}. They asked about latency. Brief took around 30 seconds on the sandbox. They're fine with it as long as it's ready before the call. Suggested pre-generating briefs from the calendar.

notes.subject: Questions from the demo
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, answers to the open questions from today: 1) yes, permissions follow your team structure, 2) briefs are cached and refresh when new notes arrive, 3) data export is available anytime in CSV.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: Call with {first_name}. Their manager wants to see it with 50 of their real contacts before deciding. Agreed to a limited proof of concept.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name} {last_name}. Very quiet during the session, hard to read. At the end asked only about price. Need to dig deeper on value next time.
Hard to read {first_name}. Ask open questions next time, find out what they actually care about.

notes.subject: Demo for leadership
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}, the CRO and finance. Finance asked about cost per seat and contract length. CRO asked for a reference customer. Overall positive, asked for a proposal.

notes.subject: Reference request
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, I've reached out to one of our customers with a similar team size. They agreed to a 20 min reference call. I'll send times once they confirm.

notes.subject: Reference call setup
notes.body: Confirmed reference call between {first_name} and our customer for Thursday. Briefed the customer on {company}'s main concerns: adoption and data privacy.
Reference call happened. {first_name} said it was very helpful, especially the part about rollout.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Second demo with {first_name}, this time for the SDR team. SDRs care less about history and more about quick research. Showed the account level view. Medium interest.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} asked if we can hide certain notes from the brief, like HR related or sensitive notes. Need to check with product. Possibly through note visibility settings.

notes.subject: Open question
notes.body: Can certain notes be excluded from briefs? Ask product before next call with {company}.

notes.subject: Re: Sensitive notes
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, confirmed with our product team: notes marked as private are excluded from briefs and search. Admins can configure which note types are included.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}. Showed what happens when a contact has almost no notes: the brief says there's not enough context instead of making something up. {first_name} said that's exactly what they needed to see.

notes.subject: Post demo check-in
notes.body: {first_name} hasn't logged into the sandbox yet. Gentle nudge. They said they'll try it this week.
Sandbox usage from {company}: 2 logins, 5 briefs generated. Low but not zero.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name} and the RevOps team. RevOps asked about data quality: what if notes are duplicated or contradict each other? Explained the brief cites both and flags open questions.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, thanks for bringing RevOps in. As promised, here's how the brief handles contradicting notes, with a short example. Let me know if they have more questions.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} mentioned the demo convinced the sales manager but the IT director is blocking new tools until January. Need to see if a small pilot can bypass that.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}, energy was low, Friday afternoon. Kept it short. Will follow up Monday with a summary.

notes.subject: Monday recap
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, short recap from Friday: the brief, the Q and A, and the timeline. Next step would be a small pilot. Does your team have 30 minutes this week to scope it?

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Showed {first_name} the citation feature in detail. Clicked a citation and it opened the exact note. They tested a few on their own and all matched. Trust is building.
{first_name} tried to "break" the Q and A by asking about something not in the notes. The answer said there was no information. Good moment.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo for {company}'s enablement team. They want to use briefs during onboarding for new hires. Different buyer, same product.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} asked whether the brief could include a suggested next step. Yes, it does. They hadn't noticed. Show it more clearly next time.

notes.subject: Next step suggestions
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, you asked about suggested next steps, here's a screenshot from the sandbox. The suggestion is based only on the cited notes, so reps can check why it's suggested.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name} who joined late. Covered basics only. Plan a follow-up for deeper questions.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: Spoke with {first_name}. The sales manager compared us with Nimbalo during the demo and preferred our UI. Price will decide.
Price will be the deciding factor at {company}. Prepare options.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name} on site. Projected on their big screen for the whole team. Reps started asking "can it tell me X about my account" and we answered live. Strong demo.

notes.subject: Great session today
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, thanks for hosting us. The team asked great questions. I'll send the pilot proposal by Wednesday.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} said one rep was worried the tool will be used to monitor their activity. Need to address that clearly, it's not a monitoring tool.
Address rep concern about monitoring at {company}. Emphasize the tool helps reps, it doesn't track them.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo focused on question answering. {first_name} asked "when did they last mention budget" and got the right note with date. They were impressed by the citation.

notes.subject: Demo materials
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, the deck and a one page summary for your director are attached. The summary focuses on ramp time for new reps, which you said was the top priority.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: Call with {first_name}. They want to involve legal early to avoid delays. Sent our standard terms.
Legal at {company} reviewing standard terms in parallel with the evaluation.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}. Asked how we measure quality. Showed our eval approach: golden test cases, citation validity, and checking that nothing is invented. They found that unusual and reassuring.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} wanted to know if the model runs locally or in the cloud. Explained both options. They prefer local for compliance reasons.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo for {first_name}'s team of SDRs and AEs. Good participation. One AE asked if it works with call transcripts. Yes, transcripts are just another activity type.
{first_name} requested a pricing proposal for 15 seats after the demo.

notes.subject: Recap and next steps
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, recap from today: team liked the brief and the Q and A, concerns were price and rollout effort. Next: I'll send a proposal for 15 seats with an onboarding plan.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} asked about training. Explained onboarding sessions are included. They want sessions recorded for future hires.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}. They asked how the brief decides what is "key". Explained it uses the most relevant notes for the contact and every key fact must cite one. They liked that it's explainable.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} said the sales manager wants to see the brief for a contact with messy, contradictory notes. Preparing that example for next session.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo for {first_name}'s partner team. Partners manage resellers, different workflow. Interest was moderate. Not a priority use case.

notes.subject: Demo slots
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, here are three slots for the demo next week: Tuesday 10am, Wednesday 3pm or Thursday 11am. Pick whichever works best for your team.
{first_name} picked Wednesday 3pm for the demo. Invite sent including their sales manager.

notes.subject: Demo prep
notes.body: Prep call with {first_name} before the demo. Agreed to focus on handoffs between AEs and on the Q and A. Skip admin settings.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}. Their manager asked "how do I know it didn't miss something important". Honest answer: retrieval can miss notes, which is why we measure recall and show sources. They appreciated the honesty.
Sandbox usage from {company}: 14 briefs and 31 questions in one week. Strong engagement.

notes.body: Hi {first_name}, we missed you at today's demo, hope everything is OK. Happy to reschedule, just pick a new time.

notes.body: {first_name} apologized for missing the demo, had an urgent customer issue. Rescheduled for Friday.

notes.subject: Demo

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} asked if admins can see which questions reps ask. Explained there are usage logs for admins but we don't use them to rate reps.

notes.body: Hi {first_name}, I extended your sandbox by two weeks so your team has more time to try it. Let me know if you want help loading more sample data.

notes.subject: Demo
notes.body: Demo with {first_name}'s regional managers. One manager asked for a weekly digest by email. Not available, logged as feedback.

notes.subject: Demo follow-up
notes.body: {first_name} said the team voted, 5 of 6 reps want to continue to a pilot. One prefers the current process.

notes.subject: Revised proposal
notes.body: Hi {first_name}, revised proposal attached with onboarding listed separately as requested. Total is unchanged. Let me know if finance needs anything else.

notes.subject: Proposal follow-up

notes.subject: Pilot metrics
notes.body: Pilot metrics agreed with {first_name}: brief usage before calls, prep time, citation accuracy.

notes.subject: Proposal follow-up

notes.body: {first_name} said their security team has 4 questions about data retention. Scheduled a call with our SE.

notes.subject: Final terms

Open items with {company}: DPA and start date.

notes.subject: Discovery workshop notes
notes.body:
Attendees: {first_name} {last_name} ({job_title}), their sales manager, their RevOps analyst, and me.

Context: {company} has grown from 10 to about 30 sellers in the last 18 months. They split the team into SDRs and AEs a year ago. Since then, handoffs have become the main source of friction. {first_name} opened by saying that the problem is not that people don't write notes, it's that nobody can find them when they need them.

Current process for preparing a call, as described by the sales manager:
1. Open the contact in the CRM and read the last two or three activities.
2. Search Gmail for the contact's name and the company domain.
3. Search Slack for the company name to see if anyone discussed it internally.
4. If the account had a previous owner, message that person and ask for context.
They estimate this takes between 10 and 20 minutes per call, and new reps often skip it entirely because they don't know where to look.

Pain points they mentioned, in their own words:
- "We lost a renewal because the new AE didn't know the customer had been promised a discount by the previous owner."
- "SDRs book meetings and the AE walks in blind."
- "Our notes are all over the place, some in the CRM, some in Google Docs, some in people's heads."

The RevOps analyst was the most technical person in the room. Questions from the analyst:
- Where is the data stored and who can access it?
- Does any customer data get used to train a model?
- How do we handle notes that contradict each other?
- What happens if the AI makes something up?
I answered that each statement in the brief cites the note it comes from, that data is not used for training, and that when context is missing the brief says so explicitly. The analyst wants to see this in practice before believing it, which is fair.

Budget: not defined. The sales manager thinks it would come from the enablement budget, which is reviewed in November. {first_name} believes they could get approval for a pilot without going through the full budget process if it stays under a certain amount.

Decision process: {first_name} is the champion. The sales manager has a strong opinion but the final decision is with the VP of Sales, who was not in the meeting. The VP cares mostly about ramp time for new hires, since they plan to hire 8 more reps next year.

Competition: they looked at Corvexa briefly but didn't like that it required changing their CRM workflow. No other vendor in active evaluation.

Technical requirements:
- SSO with Google Workspace.
- Sync with their CRM, which is HubSpot.
- Ability to import historical notes from Google Docs, probably via CSV export.
- Data must be deletable on request because of customer contracts.

Next steps agreed:
- I send a short recap and a proposed demo agenda by Friday.
- {first_name} shares a sample export of 100 anonymized notes so we can use realistic data in the demo.
- Demo in two weeks with the sales manager, the analyst and ideally the VP.

My read: strong pain, a real champion, an analyst who will be a tough but fair evaluator. The risk is budget timing. If we can show impact on ramp time, the VP will likely support it.

notes.subject: Long discovery call
notes.body:
Call with {first_name}, about 50 minutes. They were very open and walked me through their whole sales process, so this note is longer than usual.

{company} sells to mid size manufacturers. Sales cycles are long, between 4 and 9 months, with many stakeholders on the customer side. A typical deal involves an operations director, a plant manager, someone from procurement and sometimes the CFO. Reps need to remember who said what across many months, and that's where things break.

{first_name} gave a concrete example. Last quarter, a rep went into a final negotiation without knowing that the plant manager had raised a concern about installation downtime six months earlier. The customer brought it up again, the rep was caught off guard, and the deal slipped by a quarter. {first_name} said this kind of thing happens "at least once a month".

What they use today: a CRM with activity logging, but reps log inconsistently. Calls are recorded and transcribed by their dialer, but nobody reads transcripts after the fact. Emails are synced to the CRM only for some reps because the integration breaks often.

What they want:
- Before any meeting, a short summary of everything that happened with this contact and account.
- The ability to ask specific questions, like "has anyone talked about installation timelines with this customer".
- Confidence that the answer is based on real notes, not invented.

On that last point, {first_name} was very clear. Their previous experiment with a generic AI assistant ended badly because it produced a summary that mentioned a meeting that never happened. Since then, the sales director is very skeptical of anything AI. I explained our approach of citing every claim and refusing to answer when there's no supporting note. {first_name} said that's the only way the director would even consider it.

Volume: around 1,500 active contacts, maybe 40,000 activities over the last three years including transcripts. Transcripts can be long, some calls are over an hour. I said long content is split into smaller pieces for search, so length is not a problem.

Timeline: they want to decide before their annual planning, which starts in about 8 weeks. They would prefer a pilot with one regional team before rolling out to everyone.

Budget: {first_name} has a discretionary budget that could cover a small pilot. A full rollout would need the director's approval.

Concerns I noted:
- Skeptical director, needs proof with their own data.
- Inconsistent logging, so some contacts will have very little context. We need to show what the brief does in that case.
- Long transcripts, need to make sure the brief picks the relevant parts.

Next step: demo with their data for {first_name} and one regional manager. They'll export transcripts and notes for 20 accounts.

notes.subject: On site visit notes
notes.body:
Visited {company}'s office with our SE. Met {first_name}, the head of sales, and two senior AEs. Spent about two hours, including watching a rep prepare for a real call.

Observation of call preparation: the rep opened the CRM, scrolled through about 30 activities, opened three emails in another tab, then messaged a colleague on Slack asking "do you remember what happened with the pricing discussion at this account". The colleague answered 10 minutes later. Total prep time was about 18 minutes, and the rep still wasn't sure about the latest pricing conversation.

The head of sales said this is typical. Their senior AEs are faster because they remember their accounts, but when accounts get reassigned, all that memory is lost. They reassign around 20 percent of accounts every year due to territory changes and turnover.

The two senior AEs had different opinions:
- One said they would use a tool like this mainly for accounts they inherit.
- The other was skeptical, saying they prefer their own notes in a notebook. When asked what happens to the notebook if they leave, they laughed and said "the next person suffers".

Technical discussion with our SE and their IT contact (joined for 30 minutes):
- They use Microsoft 365, so SSO through Azure AD.
- CRM is Salesforce, fairly customized, with custom objects for site visits.
- They would want site visit notes included as an activity type.
- IT asked about where models run. Our SE explained the option to run in their environment. IT was interested because their legal team is strict about customer data.

{first_name} took us to lunch afterwards and shared more context. The company had a bad year and leadership is focused on efficiency, not on new tools. Any purchase needs a clear story about saving time or protecting revenue. The renewal that was lost last year due to missing context is a story the head of sales tells often, so that's our best angle.

Things to prepare:
- A business case focused on reassigned accounts and protected revenue.
- A demo that includes a site visit note type.
- A clear answer on data residency for their legal team.

Next steps:
- {first_name} will set up a meeting with legal to discuss data handling.
- We send the business case draft within a week.
- Tentative demo with the head of sales in three weeks.

Overall: good visit, real pain, but a cautious buyer in a tough year. The deal size will likely be small at first, and we should propose a narrow pilot.

notes.subject: Detailed answers to your questions
notes.body:
Hi {first_name},

Thanks again for the call yesterday. You asked several good questions and I promised to answer them in writing so you can share them with your team. Here they are.

1. Where does our data live?
Data is stored in a dedicated database for your organization. If you choose the self hosted option, everything runs inside your own cloud account, including the language model. If you choose our hosted option, data stays in the region you select.

2. Is our data used to train AI models?
No. Your notes are used only to answer questions and generate briefs for your own team. They are never used to train or improve any model, ours or a third party's.

3. How do you prevent made up information?
Every statement in a brief must point to one or more of your original notes. Before a brief is shown, we check that every citation refers to a note that was actually retrieved for that contact. If a statement can't be supported, it's removed or the brief clearly says there isn't enough information. Reps can click any citation to read the original note.

4. What happens when notes contradict each other?
The brief mentions both and cites both. For example, if one note says the budget is approved and a later one says it's on hold, the brief will show the most recent one and flag the contradiction as an open question. It doesn't try to guess which is true.

5. How long does it take to generate a brief?
It depends on the amount of history for the contact. Briefs are generated in the background and cached, so in practice reps open a brief that is already prepared. We can also pre-generate briefs for meetings on the calendar.

6. Can we import our old notes?
Yes. We support CSV import with validation per row. Rows with errors are reported, not silently skipped. Duplicate contacts are detected by email address.

7. What do you need from us to run a pilot?
A list of pilot users, read access to your CRM through an integration user, and about two hours of your admin's time for setup. Training for reps takes about one hour.

8. How do you measure whether it's working?
We agree on metrics before starting. Typically: how often reps open the brief before a call, how much time they report saving, and how many incorrect citations are reported. We share a weekly report during the pilot.

If any of these answers raise more questions, I'm happy to set up a call with our solutions engineer. Also, if it helps, I can join a short call with your security team to go through points 1 to 3 in more detail.

Best regards

notes.subject: Discovery call with technical lead
notes.body:
Call with {first_name}, the technical lead for sales systems at {company}. This was a deep technical conversation, around 45 minutes, so I'm writing everything down for the SE.

Their stack: Salesforce with about 60 custom fields on the contact object, Outreach for sequences, Gong for call recording, and an internal data warehouse in BigQuery. {first_name} is responsible for keeping all of these in sync and is clearly overloaded.

Their main concern is not whether the product works, but whether it adds another integration they have to maintain. They've been burned before: a previous tool required a nightly sync job that failed silently for weeks before anyone noticed.

Questions from {first_name}:
- How do we get data in? Push or pull? I said both are possible, we have connectors that pull and an API they can push to.
- What happens when a sync fails? I said failures are logged and visible in an admin page, and jobs are retried automatically. {first_name} asked whether failed jobs ever get stuck forever. I said there's a maximum number of retries, after which the job is marked as failed and an alert is raised. They want to see that in the demo.
- How do we avoid processing the same note twice? I explained that each piece of content is identified by a hash, so unchanged content isn't processed again. {first_name} liked that, said it would save them from duplicate data problems they've had before.
- Can they query the data from their warehouse? Not directly today, but there's an export. They want a scheduled export to BigQuery eventually.
- What are the API rate limits? I didn't know the exact numbers, need to confirm with the SE.

On AI specifically, {first_name} asked how retrieval works. I gave a simple explanation: notes are converted into vectors, and when you ask a question, we find the closest notes for that contact and pass only those to the model. {first_name} asked what happens if the right note isn't among the closest ones. Honest answer: the model won't see it, and that's why we measure retrieval quality separately from the final answer. They appreciated the honesty and said most vendors pretend this never happens.

Security: they need SOC 2 or equivalent documentation, and a pen test report from the last 12 months.

{first_name} is not the buyer. The buyer is the VP of Sales Operations. But {first_name} has an effective veto, if they say the integration is risky, the deal won't happen.

Next steps:
- SE to join the next call to cover sync failure handling and rate limits.
- Send security documentation.
- {first_name} to share their integration checklist that every vendor must pass.

My take: {first_name} is skeptical but fair. If we pass their checklist, they could become a strong internal ally.

notes.subject: Demo notes with full team
notes.body:
Demo for {company}. Attendees: {first_name} {last_name}, their VP of Sales, two sales managers, four AEs and one SDR. About 60 minutes.

I started with their problem in their own words from discovery: reps spend too long preparing, and context gets lost when accounts change hands. The VP nodded at that, which was a good sign.

First part: the contact timeline. I showed a contact with about 40 activities across calls, emails and meetings. The AEs immediately started comparing it to their own process. One AE said it's what they wish the CRM looked like.

Second part: the brief. I generated a brief live. It took about 35 seconds, which created a slightly awkward pause. I explained that in real use briefs are pre-generated. The brief showed a summary, key facts with citations, open questions and a suggested next step. I clicked on a citation and it opened the original note. The VP asked me to click on another one, then another. All matched. That moment built a lot of trust.

Third part: the Q and A. I let the team ask questions. Questions they asked:
- "What did they say about the budget last time?" Answer cited an email from two weeks earlier.
- "Who is the decision maker?" Answer listed two names with citations to meeting notes.
- "Did they ever mention a competitor?" Answer said no competitor was mentioned in the available notes. One AE said that was correct.
- "What is their favorite football team?" Answer said there was no information about that. People laughed but the VP said that's exactly the behavior they need.

Concerns raised:
- One manager asked about rep adoption. Past tools failed because reps didn't use them. I suggested sending the brief link automatically before each meeting.
- The SDR asked if it works for cold prospects with no history. Honest answer: no, the value comes from existing history. For cold prospects, the brief will say there's not enough context.
- The VP asked about cost. I gave a range and said we'd send a proposal after scoping.

After the demo, the VP stayed for 10 more minutes and asked about a pilot. They want to start with one team of 8 reps for 6 weeks. Success criteria the VP proposed: reps open the brief before at least half of their calls, and the managers see better prepared reps in call reviews.

Next steps:
- Send pilot proposal by Wednesday.
- {first_name} to identify the pilot team.
- Set up integration with their CRM in the sandbox.

Overall: the best demo I've had this month. The citation moment and the "no information" answers did more than any slide.

notes.subject: Demo with skeptical director
notes.body:
Demo with {first_name} and their sales director, who {first_name} warned me is very skeptical about AI tools. About 45 minutes.

The director started by saying they had tried two AI products last year and both "invented things". They were clear that if they saw a single made up fact, the meeting would be over. Honestly, I liked that framing because it plays to our strength.

I skipped most of the slides and went directly to the product with {company}'s sample data, which {first_name} had sent us last week.

The director picked a contact they knew very well and asked me to generate a brief. While it generated, they wrote down on paper what they expected to see. When the brief appeared, they compared it line by line with their notes. Results:
- The summary was accurate.
- Three of the four key facts matched what the director expected.
- One key fact was something the director had forgotten, a request for a payment plan made eight months ago. They clicked the citation, read the note, and said "I completely forgot about that".
- The open questions section mentioned that the contract renewal date was not confirmed in any note, which was true.

Then the director tried to break it. They asked questions designed to trick the system:
- "When did they agree to the 30 percent discount?" There was no such agreement. The answer said no note mentions a 30 percent discount, and cited the note where a 10 percent discount was discussed.
- "Summarize the meeting from last Friday." There was no meeting. The answer said there's no record of a meeting on that date.
- They asked the same question in a slightly different way three times. Answers were consistent.

After that, the director's tone changed. They said this was the first time an AI tool admitted it didn't know something. They asked about how we test this. I explained that we have a test set of contacts with known facts, and we measure whether citations are valid and whether answers contain unsupported claims. The director wants to see those numbers.

Concerns still open:
- The director wants to know the error rate in numbers, not anecdotes.
- They want to make sure reps can't modify the brief and present it as fact to customers.
- Price wasn't discussed yet.

Next steps:
- Send the director a summary of our evaluation method and results.
- {first_name} will organize a test with 10 more contacts chosen by the director.
- If the test goes well, proposal for a pilot.

This is a very good sign. The director went from hostile to curious in 45 minutes.

- The sales manager liked that citations open the original note, so they can verify before trusting.
- The VP was impressed that the tool said "no information" instead of guessing.
- Two reps said they would use it every day if it was ready before their meetings without clicking anything.

Negative feedback:
- Generation time was mentioned by almost everyone. 30 to 40 seconds feels long during a live demo. I explained pre-generation and caching again, but {first_name} suggested we show that next time instead of generating live.
- One rep found the summary "too generic" for a contact with very few notes. That's expected, but we should explain better that the brief is only as good as the history.
- The SDR team doesn't see much value, since they work mostly with new leads.
- One manager asked whether the tool could be used to evaluate reps based on what they ask. {first_name} wants a clear statement that we don't do that.

Questions that came up after the demo:
- Can the brief be exported to PDF for offline use? I don't think so today, need to check.
- Can managers see briefs for their team's contacts? Yes, permissions follow the team structure.
- What happens with notes written in Spanish? Some of their reps write in Spanish. Need to check quality.
- Is there a limit to how many briefs can be generated per day? Need to confirm with product.

Politics:
- {first_name} said the VP is ready to approve a pilot, but procurement will want three quotes. {first_name} will handle that.
- The SDR manager might push back on the cost if their team is included. Suggest excluding SDRs from the pilot.

Next steps:
- I send answers to the four open questions by Thursday.
- I prepare a pilot proposal for AEs only, 10 seats, 6 weeks.
- {first_name} starts the procurement process in parallel to save time.

My assessment: high probability of a pilot. Risk is procurement timing and the price comparison with the other quotes.

notes.subject: Follow-up on demo questions
notes.body:
Hi {first_name},

Thank you and your team for the time on Tuesday. Below are answers to the questions that came up during and after the demo. I've grouped them by topic.

Performance
You noticed that generating a brief live took around 30 seconds. In normal use, briefs are generated in the background as soon as new activity arrives, and they're cached until something changes. We can also generate them automatically for meetings on your calendar, so reps open a brief that's already ready. We'll make sure the pilot is configured that way.

Accuracy
Each statement in the brief and in answers cites the original notes. Before a brief is shown, we check that every citation points to a note that was actually used to generate it. If something can't be supported, it's not shown. We also maintain a set of test contacts with known facts and run evaluations regularly. I'm attaching a summary of the latest results so your sales director can see the numbers.

Privacy and rep monitoring
Admins can see usage statistics, like how many briefs were generated. We don't provide reports that rank reps by what they ask, and we don't recommend using the tool for performance evaluation. I'd be happy to say this directly to your team during the pilot kickoff.

Languages
Some of your reps write notes in Spanish. Summaries work well with mixed languages in our tests, but question answering is slightly less accurate. I'd suggest including a few Spanish speaking reps in the pilot so we can measure it with your real data.

Export
Exporting a brief to PDF isn't available today. Reps can copy the brief or share a link with colleagues who have access. I've passed the PDF request to our product team.

Limits
There's no hard daily limit on briefs for your plan size. If usage is unusually high, briefs are queued and generated in order, so nothing is lost.

Next steps
I'll send the pilot proposal for 10 AEs by Thursday. If your procurement team needs our vendor information in advance, let me know and I'll send it today.

Best regards

notes.subject: Second demo for IT and security
notes.body:
Second demo for {company}, this time for IT and security. Attendees: {first_name}, their IT manager, a security engineer and our SE. This was less about the product and more about architecture and risk.

Our SE walked through the architecture:
- Application layer that receives requests and validates input.
- Background workers that process new notes: splitting long notes into pieces, generating vectors, and storing them.
- A database with vector search, filtered by contact and account so one customer's data is never mixed with another.
- The language model, which can run in their environment or ours.
- A logging layer that records every model call: which model, how long it took, which notes were used, and whether the citations were valid.

Security engineer's questions:
- Can a note contain text that tricks the model into ignoring its instructions? Our SE said yes, that's a real risk called prompt injection. Notes are treated as data, not instructions, and the output is validated against a schema. Citations that point to notes not retrieved are rejected. The engineer asked for test cases, our SE said we include injection attempts in our evaluation set.
- Where are the logs stored and for how long? Our SE said logs stay in the same environment as the data and retention is configurable.
- Is there any outbound traffic to third parties? With the self hosted option, no. With hosted, only to our infrastructure.
- How are secrets managed? Environment variables in their secret manager, never in code.

IT manager's questions:
- What do they need to run the self hosted option? Container runtime, a PostgreSQL database with the vector extension, and enough CPU or GPU for the model. Our SE said a small model can run on CPU but it's slower.
- How do updates work? New container images, they decide when to deploy.
- Who supports it if something breaks? We do, under the support agreement.

The security engineer was clearly experienced and asked good, specific questions. At the end, they said they were "cautiously positive" and want to see our evaluation results, specifically the injection tests.

{first_name} told me after the meeting that this was the hardest gate, and it went well.

Action items:
- SE sends architecture diagram and the injection test summary.
- I send the security questionnaire responses.
- IT manager to confirm whether they prefer hosted or self hosted.

Risk: if they choose self hosted, the implementation will take longer and their IT team will need to be involved, which could delay the pilot by a few weeks.

notes.subject: Proposal review meeting notes
notes.body:
Proposal review with {first_name}, their finance manager and their sales director. About 50 minutes. The proposal was for 20 seats, annual term, onboarding included.

The sales director opened by saying they're happy with the product and the pilot. The meeting was mostly about money and risk.

Finance manager's points:
- The price per seat is higher than what they budgeted. They budgeted based on another vendor's list price, which is lower.
- They prefer quarterly payments instead of annual upfront, because of cash flow this year.
- They asked whether the onboarding fee could be waived.
- They want a clear exit option if adoption is low after six months.

Sales director's points:
- They want all 20 seats active from day one, not a phased rollout.
- They care more about adoption than price, but they need finance on board.
- They asked if we could guarantee a response time for support issues.

{first_name} mostly listened, but at one point reminded everyone that the pilot showed prep time going from about 15 minutes to 6. That helped frame the conversation around value instead of cost.

What I said:
- On price, I didn't offer a discount in the meeting. I said I'd come back with options.
- On quarterly payments, I said it's possible but may affect the annual rate.
- On onboarding, I explained that it's the main driver of adoption and I'd rather keep it.
- On the exit option, I said we could include an adoption review at month six with agreed metrics.
- On support, I confirmed our standard response times.

After the meeting, I talked to my manager. Options we can offer:
1. Keep 20 seats, 2 year term, 10 percent discount, quarterly payments.
2. Keep 20 seats, 1 year term, no discount, quarterly payments, onboarding included.
3. Start with 15 seats at the 1 year price and add 5 later at the same rate.

My read on the people:
- Finance is the main obstacle, but not hostile. They need a number they can defend.
- The sales director is ready to buy and will push internally.
- {first_name} is a strong champion, well respected by the director.

Risks:
- If finance compares only on price with the other vendor, we lose.
- Their fiscal quarter ends in five weeks. If we don't sign before, the budget might be reallocated.

Next steps:
- Send the three options in writing by tomorrow.
- Offer a call with finance alone to walk through the options.
- Ask {first_name} which option the director prefers before sending, so we lead with that one.

notes.subject: Pilot proposal details
notes.body:
Hi {first_name},

As promised, here's the pilot proposal for {company}. I've tried to keep it short and concrete so it's easy to share with your director.

Scope
- 10 account executives from one regional team.
- Duration of 6 weeks, starting the Monday after setup is complete.
- Access to the brief, question answering, and the activity timeline.
- Historical notes from the last 12 months imported from your CRM.

Setup
- Week 0: SSO configuration, CRM integration and historical import. We'll need about two hours from your admin.
- Day 1 of the pilot: a one hour training session for the 10 reps, recorded for anyone who can't attend.
- Briefs pre-generated for meetings on reps' calendars, so they're ready before each call.

Success criteria
We suggest measuring three things, and we'll report on them weekly:
1. Usage: reps open the brief before at least 60 percent of their external meetings.
2. Time saved: reps report their average preparation time at the start and end of the pilot.
3. Accuracy: number of incorrect citations reported by reps. Target is zero.
At the end, we'll review the results together with your director and decide on next steps.

Cost
The pilot has a fixed cost, which is fully credited if you sign an annual agreement within 30 days of the pilot ending. If you decide not to continue, there's no further obligation.

What we need from you
- Names and emails of the 10 pilot reps.
- An integration user in your CRM with read access.
- A contact in IT for SSO setup.
- 30 minutes with your director at the start to align on success criteria.

Data
All data from the pilot stays in your selected region. If you don't continue, we delete all your data within 30 days and send written confirmation.

Timeline
If we receive the signed pilot agreement this week, setup can happen next week and the pilot can start the week after.

Let me know if you'd like to adjust anything, especially the success criteria. It's important that they reflect what your director cares about.

Best regards

notes.subject: Pilot results review
notes.body:
Pilot results review with {first_name}, their sales director and two pilot reps. About 45 minutes. This was the end of the 6 week pilot.

Numbers we presented:
- Usage: reps opened the brief before 68 percent of external meetings. Target was 60.
- Time saved: average self reported prep time went from 14 minutes to 5.
- Questions asked: 214 in total, most common topics were last objections, pricing history, and who the decision makers are.
- Accuracy: 2 citations were reported as incorrect. We investigated both. In one case, the note had been logged on the wrong contact in the CRM. In the other, the citation pointed to the right note but the summary sentence was too broad. We fixed the prompt and re-ran the test set.

Rep feedback:
- One rep said the most valuable moment was when the brief reminded them that a customer had asked for a specific integration a year ago. They brought it up in the call and the customer was impressed.
- The other rep said they use the Q and A more than the brief, mostly in the 5 minutes before a call.
- Both said generation was sometimes slow when they asked a question for a contact without a pre-generated brief.
- One rep found the suggested next step "a bit obvious" sometimes.

Director's reaction:
- Very positive about usage and time saved.
- Asked directly about the two citation errors. I explained them openly. The director said they appreciated the transparency and that two issues in 214 questions, both explained, was acceptable.
- Wants to roll out to the whole sales team, about 35 people.
- Asked if the CS team could join later.

Open topics:
- Price for 35 seats. Director expects a volume discount.
- Rollout plan for the other teams.
- Whether to include Spanish speaking reps, since pilot reps all wrote in English.

Next steps:
- Send a proposal for 35 seats with a volume discount and a phased rollout plan.
- Share a written pilot report the director can forward to leadership.
- Schedule a call with the CS lead next month.

Overall: the pilot succeeded. The honest handling of the citation errors seemed to increase trust rather than reduce it.

notes.subject: Negotiation meeting with procurement
notes.body:
Negotiation with {company}'s procurement team. Attendees: {first_name}, a procurement manager, and my sales director joined from our side. About an hour, and tense at times.

The procurement manager started by saying they had three proposals and ours was the most expensive by a significant margin. They asked for a 30 percent discount to "stay in the process".

My director stayed calm and asked what the other proposals included. Procurement didn't share details but admitted that one of them didn't include onboarding, and the other had no option to run models in their own environment.

Main points of the discussion:

Price
- Procurement asked for 30 percent. We said that wasn't possible.
- We offered 10 percent for a 2 year commitment.
- Procurement countered with 20 percent and a 1 year term.
- We ended at 12 percent for 2 years, or 5 percent for 1 year, pending their internal decision.

Payment terms
- They asked for net 90. Our standard is net 30.
- We agreed to net 45 as a compromise.

Onboarding
- Procurement asked to remove onboarding to lower the price. {first_name} intervened and said the sales team needs the onboarding. Procurement accepted keeping it.

Exit clause
- They want to be able to terminate after 12 months even on a 2 year deal.
- My director said we could allow termination at month 12 with 90 days notice, but then the discount would be adjusted to the 1 year rate retroactively. Procurement said they'd need to check with legal.

Liability
- Procurement mentioned their legal team will send redlines on the liability clause. We asked to receive them as soon as possible to avoid delays.

At one point, the procurement manager said that if we couldn't reach 20 percent, they'd recommend the cheaper vendor. {first_name} later told me privately that this is a standard tactic and the sales director has already said they want our product.

After the meeting, my director and I agreed:
- We won't go beyond 12 percent.
- We can be flexible on payment terms and the exit clause.
- We should help {first_name} prepare a justification document for procurement that focuses on total value, including onboarding and the self hosted option.

Next steps:
- Send revised terms in writing today.
- Prepare the value justification document with {first_name}.
- Wait for legal redlines.

Risk level: medium. Procurement is tough, but the business side wants us.

notes.subject: Long negotiation call
notes.body:
Call with {first_name}, around 40 minutes. They called to explain where things stand internally, and it's more complicated than I thought.

Situation inside {company}:
- The sales director wants to sign with us.
- The CFO has asked every department to cut software spending by 15 percent this year.
- The sales department already pays for 7 tools. The CFO asked why they need an eighth.
- {first_name} has been asked to show which existing tool we would replace, or to prove that we pay for ourselves within six months.

What {first_name} needs from me:
1. A short ROI calculation using the pilot numbers.
2. An argument about which tool, or part of a tool, we could replace.
3. Flexibility on price or terms to make the CFO more comfortable.

We worked through the ROI together on the call:
- 25 reps, each with about 12 external meetings per week.
- Pilot showed prep time dropping by about 8 minutes per meeting.
- That's around 40 hours per week across the team.
- {first_name} said the CFO doesn't care about hours, they care about revenue. So we added the story of the renewal that was saved during the pilot. That single renewal was worth more than our annual price.

On replacing a tool:
- They pay for a note taking plugin that reps barely use, because notes end up in the CRM anyway.
- {first_name} thinks they could cancel it if our product covers summaries of call transcripts.
- I confirmed that call transcripts can be imported as activities and summarized in the brief.

On flexibility:
- I said I can't lower the price further without my director, but I can propose a 6 month adoption review with the option to reduce seats if usage is low.
- {first_name} thought that would help a lot, because it limits the CFO's risk.

{first_name} also mentioned that their fiscal year ends in 6 weeks, and the CFO wants all decisions made before then. If not, the budget conversation starts again from zero.

Next steps:
- I send the ROI one pager by tomorrow.
- I propose the adoption review clause in writing.
- {first_name} presents both to the CFO on Thursday.

My assessment: the deal is at risk, but {first_name} is fighting for it. Our best chance is the replacement argument plus the low risk clause.

notes.subject: Response to legal redlines
notes.body:
Hi {first_name},

Our legal team has reviewed the redlines your legal counsel sent last week. Below is a summary of our response to each point so you can follow along. The full marked up document is attached.

1. Limitation of liability
Your team asked to raise the liability cap from 12 months of fees to 24 months. We can accept 18 months as a compromise. We can't accept unlimited liability for data breaches, but we can carve out a higher cap specifically for breaches caused by our negligence.

2. Termination for convenience
You asked for termination for convenience with 30 days notice. We can accept termination for convenience after the first 12 months with 90 days notice. If termination happens before the end of the 2 year term, the discount adjusts to the 1 year rate for the remaining period.

3. Data processing
We accept your data processing addendum with one change: we need to keep the list of sub-processors as a link that we update, rather than fixed in the contract, with 30 days notice of any change.

4. Data deletion
We accept your requirement to delete all data within 30 days of termination and to provide written confirmation.

5. Service levels
We accept adding the support response times to the contract: 4 hours for critical issues and 1 business day for normal issues. We can't accept financial penalties for uptime below 99.5 percent, but we can offer service credits.

6. Governing law
We propose the law of the jurisdiction in our standard agreement. If this is a blocker for your team, we can discuss a neutral option.

7. Assignment
We accept that neither party can assign the contract without the other's consent, except in the case of a merger or acquisition.

8. Insurance
We can provide our certificate of insurance. Our coverage meets the minimums your team requested.

I think we're close. The main open topics are the liability carve out and governing law. Would it help to set up a 30 minute call between both legal teams this week? In my experience, that resolves these points faster than going back and forth by email.

Thanks for your patience with the process.

Best regards

notes.subject: Final negotiation meeting
notes.body:
Final negotiation meeting with {first_name}, their VP of Sales and their procurement lead. My director joined as well. About 35 minutes. Goal was to close the remaining open points.

Open points coming into the meeting:
1. Discount level.
2. Number of seats.
3. Start date.
4. Training sessions.

Discussion:

Discount
- Procurement asked one last time for 15 percent. We held at 12 percent for a 2 year term. The VP said they were fine with 12 and asked procurement to move on. That settled it.

Seats
- They wanted 30 seats but asked whether 5 could be read only for managers at a lower price. We agreed to 25 full seats and 5 read only seats.

Start date
- They wanted to start after their sales kickoff, which is in 5 weeks. We agreed on a start date right after the kickoff, with setup during the 2 weeks before so reps can start using it immediately after the event.
- The VP asked if we could present the tool during their sales kickoff. We said yes, a 20 minute session.

Training
- They asked for 2 additional training sessions beyond the standard onboarding. We agreed at no extra cost.

Other topics:
- The VP asked about the roadmap, specifically calendar based pre-generation. I said it's available now in a basic form and improving. I was careful not to commit to dates for anything that isn't released.
- Procurement confirmed the legal review is complete and the contract can be issued today.

Final terms:
- 25 full seats and 5 read only seats.
- 2 year term with 12 percent discount.
- Quarterly billing, net 45.
- Onboarding included plus 2 additional training sessions.
- Start date right after their sales kickoff.
- 20 minute presentation at their kickoff.

Next steps:
- I send the final contract today.
- {first_name} coordinates signatures, VP is the signer.
- Kickoff planning call next week.

My director said this was a well run negotiation. The key was that the VP wanted the product and procurement eventually accepted that.

notes.subject: Deal at risk
notes.body:
Difficult call with {first_name}. About 30 minutes. The deal is at risk and I want to capture everything while it's fresh.

What happened:
- Their company announced a reorganization yesterday. The sales team will be merged with another business unit.
- The new head of the combined unit hasn't been named yet.
- All pending purchases above a certain amount are paused until the new head is in place, which could take 4 to 8 weeks.
- {first_name} is not sure if their own role will change.

What {first_name} told me about the deal:
- The contract was ready for signature. Only the VP's signature was missing.
- The VP doesn't want to sign something the new head might cancel.
- {first_name} still believes in the product and will present it to the new head.

What we discussed as options:
1. Wait until the new head is named and start the conversation again. Risk: new priorities, new budget review.
2. Sign a smaller agreement now, below the approval threshold. Around 10 seats for 1 year. Risk: smaller deal, but it keeps us inside.
3. Extend the pilot for free for one month to keep usage going. Risk: free usage without commitment, but it keeps reps engaged and creates internal demand.

{first_name} liked option 2 the most, possibly combined with a short extension of the current pilot users. They'll check if 10 seats falls under the threshold.

Things I need to watch:
- Keep pricing for the full deal valid for 90 days, so we can expand quickly once the new head is in place.
- Avoid putting pressure on {first_name}, who is clearly stressed about the reorganization.
- Identify who else in the combined unit might support us. {first_name} mentioned a sales manager from the other unit who saw our demo at a conference.

Next steps:
- {first_name} checks the approval threshold and replies by Friday.
- I prepare a 10 seat, 1 year agreement as a backup.
- I extend the pilot users' access by 2 weeks to avoid an interruption.

My assessment: probability dropped from high to medium. If option 2 works, we can still save most of the value later.

notes.subject: Kickoff meeting notes
notes.body:
Kickoff meeting with {company} after signing. Attendees: {first_name} (project lead on their side), their CRM admin, their sales enablement manager, our onboarding manager and me. About 60 minutes.

Goals for the first 30 days, agreed in the meeting:
1. All 25 reps trained and active within the first two weeks.
2. Historical notes from the last 24 months imported.
3. Briefs pre-generated for all external meetings on reps' calendars.
4. Weekly usage report sent to {first_name} and the sales director.

Technical setup plan:
- Week 1: SSO configuration with their identity provider. CRM integration with a dedicated integration user. Test import with 500 notes to check formatting and dates.
- Week 2: Full historical import. Our onboarding manager estimated around 50,000 activities, including call transcripts. Processing will run in the background and should finish within a couple of days.
- Week 2: Calendar integration for pre-generation.
- Week 3: Training sessions, split into two groups by time zone.

Risks discussed:
- Data quality: the CRM admin warned that some old notes are attached to the wrong contacts because of a past migration. We agreed to import them anyway and fix issues as reps report them, rather than delay the project.
- Duplicate contacts: about 5 percent of contacts are duplicates with different capitalization in the email. Our import normalizes emails, so duplicates will be detected. The admin was relieved.
- Long transcripts: some calls are over 90 minutes. Our onboarding manager explained that long content is split into smaller pieces and processed separately, so it doesn't cause problems.

Training plan from the enablement manager:
- Session 1: opening a brief and understanding citations. Emphasis on clicking citations to verify.
- Session 2: asking good questions. Examples from their own accounts.
- A cheat sheet and a recorded video for new hires.

Communication:
- Weekly 30 minute check-in for the first month.
- A shared Slack channel between our team and theirs.
- {first_name} is the single point of contact for decisions.

{first_name} mentioned that the sales director will present early results at the next quarterly business review, in about 10 weeks, so it's important to have clear numbers by then.

Next steps:
- CRM admin creates the integration user by Wednesday.
- Our onboarding manager sends the SSO configuration guide today.
- Test import on Friday.

notes.subject: Quarterly business review
notes.body:
Quarterly business review with {first_name}, their sales director and their CS lead. About 50 minutes. This was the first QBR after go live.

Usage numbers for the quarter:
- 24 of 25 reps active at least once a week.
- Around 1,900 briefs generated, most of them pre-generated from calendar events.
- Around 3,200 questions asked.
- Reps opened a brief before about 70 percent of external meetings.

Quality:
- 5 citation issues reported in the quarter. All 5 were caused by notes attached to the wrong contact in their CRM, which we flagged during onboarding. The admin has been cleaning those up.
- No cases of made up information reported.
- One complaint about a brief that said "not enough context" for an important contact. The cause was that the rep stored most notes in a personal document, not in the CRM.

Business impact, as reported by the sales director:
- New hires are running customer calls alone about three weeks earlier than before.
- Two renewals were saved because reps found past commitments in the brief.
- Managers say call reviews are more productive because reps arrive prepared.

Feedback and requests:
- The sales director wants a report of accounts with no activity in the last 60 days. We logged it as a feature request.
- Reps asked for faster answers when there's no pre-generated brief.
- The CS lead wants to use briefs for renewal calls and asked about pricing for 10 CS seats.
- {first_name} asked for better support for notes in Spanish, since they're hiring in Latin America.

Our commitments:
- Share a written summary of the QBR within two days.
- Send a quote for 10 CS seats.
- Run a test with Spanish notes and share the results.
- Investigate the latency for questions without a pre-generated brief.

The sales director closed the meeting by saying the tool is now "part of how we prepare for calls", which is the best outcome we could hope for at this stage.

Expansion potential: CS team now, possibly the Latin America team in two quarters.

notes.subject: Onboarding summary and next steps
notes.body:
Hi {first_name},

Now that onboarding is complete, I wanted to send a summary of where we are and what comes next. Feel free to share it with your director.

What was completed
- SSO configured and tested with your identity provider.
- CRM integration running every few minutes, with failures reported in the admin page.
- Historical import of about 48,000 activities from the last 24 months. Around 300 rows were rejected because of missing dates or invalid contact references. The report with those rows was sent to your CRM admin.
- Duplicate detection merged about 900 contacts that had the same email with different capitalization or extra spaces.
- Calendar integration active for all 25 reps, so briefs are prepared before external meetings.
- Two training sessions delivered, with 23 of 25 reps attending live. Recordings are available for the rest.

Early usage
- In the first two weeks, 21 reps generated at least one brief.
- The most common questions were about previous objections, pricing discussions and decision makers.
- No incorrect citations reported so far.

Known issues

What comes next
